Article.ArticleTitle: Effects of primary somatosensory cortex high-definition transcranial direct current stimulation combined with core stability training on pain and glutamate levels and neuromuscular function in chronic low back pain: a randomized controlled trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Chronic low back pain (CLBP) involves pain-related changes in sensory processing, motor control, and broader neurobiological function. The primary somatosensory cortex (S1) is a relevant neuromodulation target because it contributes to sensory-discriminative pain processing and exhibits maladaptive plasticity in chronic pain states. However, S1-targeted high-definition transcranial direct current stimulation (HD-tDCS) has been insufficiently studied in CLBP.

To determine whether S1-targeted HD-tDCS combined with core stability training reduces pain intensity and pain-related disability in adults with CLBP, and to explore associated changes in paraspinal muscle biomechanical properties, resting-state EEG activity, and serum metabolites.

In this randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial, 36 adults with CLBP received active or sham S1 HD-tDCS combined with a standardized 4-week core stability training program. Pain-related scale was assessed using the VAS, ODI, RMDQ and FABQ. Secondary outcomes included biomechanical properties of the lumbar erector spinae and multifidus measured using MyotonPRO. Exploratory outcomes included resting-state electroencephalographic alpha-band power spectral density (PSD) and phase-locking value (PLV) connectivity, as well as untargeted serum metabolomics in a subset of participants.

Compared with sham stimulation, active S1 HD-tDCS was associated with greater reductions in VAS, ODI, RMDQ and FABQ scores after treatment. The active group also showed larger decreases in lumbar erector spinae and multifidus tone and stiffness, along with greater improvement in elasticity. Resting-state EEG demonstrated increased alpha-band PSD across frontal, central, and parieto-occipital regions and reduced alpha-band PLV connectivity after active stimulation. In the metabolomics subset, active treatment was associated with greater reductions in circulating L-glutamate and enrichment of ferroptosis-related pathways. Changes in pain intensity were correlated with changes in paraspinal muscle stiffness, central alpha-band PSD, and L-glutamate levels.

S1-targeted HD-tDCS combined with core stability training may improve short-term pain intensity and pain-related disability in adults with CLBP. The accompanying muscular, electrophysiological, and metabolomic findings were consistent with the clinical changes. These findings support S1-targeted HD-tDCS as a potential adjunct to exercise-based rehabilitation in CLBP.

Journal.Title: Journal of health, population, and nutrition

Article.ArticleTitle: The effect of early rehabilitation nursing on the recovery of cardiac function in patients with acute myocardial infarction.

Abstract.AbstractText: This study aimed to investigate the effect of implementing early rehabilitation nursing on the recovery of cardiac function indices and prognosis after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) treatment in patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI).

Patients diagnosed with AMI and treated with PCI between March 2020 and May 2024 were selected as the study participants. This was a prospective randomised controlled trial; patients were randomly allocated to an observation group and a control group using a random number table method (157 cases per group). The control group received routine nursing after surgery, whereas the observation group received structured early rehabilitation nursing. After 6 months of intervention, cardiac function indices, the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and quality of life were compared between the two groups. Cardiac function indices included stroke volume (SV), left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV) and 6-minute walking distance (6MWD). The World Health Organization Quality of Life Measurement Brief Form was used to evaluate quality of life.

After nursing intervention, the levels of SV, LVEF and 6MWD in the cardiac function indices of the observation group were higher than those of the control group, whereas the levels of LVEDV were lower than those of the control group; the differences between the two groups were significant (p < 0.05). The total incidence of MACE in the observation group was lower than that in the control group (p < 0.05). In the comparison of quality-of-life scores, the observation group scored higher than the control group in five domains (p < 0.05).
Early rehabilitation nursing for patients with AMI can effectively improve patients' cardiac function indices and reduce the risk of MACE, thereby improving their quality of life.

Article.ArticleTitle: Effect of a free sugar-restricted diet on anthropometric parameters, lipid profile, and glycemic control in women with polycystic ovary syndrome: a randomized controlled trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: High-sugar diets rich in fructose and other simple sugars are associated with increased lipogenesis and insulin resistance, potentially increasing the risk of metabolic syndrome, a condition closely linked with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). This study aimed to evaluate the effects of a free sugar-restricted diet on anthropometric parameters, lipid profile, and glycemic control in women with PCOS.

In this randomized controlled clinical trial, 74 women aged 18-45 years with diagnosed PCOS were randomly assigned to either a free sugar-restricted diet group (n = 37) or a standard diet group (n = 37) for 12 weeks. Anthropometric indices, fasting blood glucose (FBG), serum insulin, insulin (HOMA-IR), insulin sensitivity (QUICKI), and lipid profile parameters including triglycerides (TG), total cholesterol (TC), low-density lipoprotein (LDL), and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol were measured at baseline and at the end of the study.

Compared to the control group, the intervention group showed significant reductions in body weight and body mass index (BMI) (P = 0.017 and P = 0.026, respectively). There was a significant reduction in FBG (P < 0.001) and an increase in QUICKI (P = 0.022) in the intervention group in comparison with control, though QUICKI lost significance after adjusting for confounders. Both groups experienced significant reductions in TC and LDL during 12 weeks, while TG levels decreased significantly only in the intervention group (P = 0.001). Between-group comparisons revealed a significant difference in TG (P = 0.037), and a near-significant difference in LDL (P = 0.054). After adjusting for confounders, lipid profile components, except for LDL, improved in the intervention group.
This study showed that a 12-week free sugar-restricted diet can lead to weight reduction and improvements in blood glucose and lipid profile parameters in women with PCOS.

Journal.Title: Archives of orthopaedic and trauma surgery

Article.ArticleTitle: Closed reduction in distal radius fractures: manual manipulation vs. finger trap traction-a prospective randomized controlled clinical trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Initial treatment of distal radius fractures (DRF) can be either performed without reduction or with a reduction method as finger-trap traction (FTT) only or by additional manual reduction (MR) under hematoma block. There is no clear evidence on which reduction method is superior, however, MR is more invasive and seems to lead to higher pain levels and more post reduction complications. The objective of this study was to evaluate the clinical relevance of MR compared to FTT in acute DRFs.

Study design was a prospective, single-centre, balanced randomized [1:1], and parallel grouped, controlled trial. Inclusion criteria were patients with a DRF type A2, A3 or C according to the AO classification and a dorsal tilt of ≥ 10°. The patients were randomized either in the FTT or in the MR group. Depending on the patient's functional demand and the fracture configuration, conservative or operative treatment was initiated. Over one year, clinical and radiological data were assessed at six follow-ups.

A total of 53 patients were included. Regarding radiological results neither FTT nor MR achieved sufficient reduction results (median dorsal tilt was - 16 to -18 after one year) and none of the techniques was superior. The clinical results between the conservatively treated groups were comparable and showed no significant difference. Complications included one CRPS in the conservative MR group, one CRPS after FTT and operation, one secondary carpal tunnel syndrome in the conservative FTT group and one skin lesion after MR.

Manual reduction under haematoma block showed no benefit. In patients with AO type A2, A3 and type C fractures and a dorsal tilt ≥ 10° only FTT (if required under a haematoma block or comparable analgesia) is recommended regardless of whether surgery is performed or not.
Level I randomized controlled trial.

Article.ArticleTitle: Effects of a Nurse-Led Multicomponent Exercise Intervention for Haemodialysis Patients With Possible or Confirmed Sarcopenia: A Cluster Randomised Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: To assess the potential effects, safety and feasibility of a nurse-led multicomponent exercise intervention on skeletal muscle function and quality of life in haemodialysis patients with possible or confirmed sarcopenia.
A cluster randomised trial with clusters defined by fixed haemodialysis schedules.

A total of 56 eligible participants were enrolled and allocated through cluster randomisation. The intervention group (n = 28) received a 12-week nurse-led multicomponent exercise intervention in addition to standard care, whereas the control group (n = 28) received standard care. The primary outcomes included skeletal muscle mass index (SMI), handgrip strength, gait speed and short physical performance battery (SPPB) scores. Secondary outcomes included scores on the Kidney Disease Quality of Life 36-Item Short-Form Survey (KDQOL-36) and C-reactive protein levels. Handgrip strength, gait speed, SPPB scores and KDQOL-36 scores were assessed at baseline and at Weeks 4, 8 and 12 during the intervention period, whereas SMI and C-reactive protein were assessed at baseline and Week 12. An intention-to-treat analysis was employed, and the effects of the intervention were evaluated using linear mixed models.

Of the 56 participants, 50 completed the study. The intervention group showed favourable trends in handgrip strength, gait speed and SPPB scores, with moderate-to-large effect sizes; however, these differences were not statistically significant after Bonferroni correction. Furthermore, no significant between-group differences were found in skeletal muscle mass index, health-related quality of life, or C-reactive protein levels. No serious intervention-related adverse events were reported.

The nurse-led multicomponent exercise intervention was safe and feasible and showed favourable trends in muscle strength and physical function, although statistically significant between-group differences were not retained after correction for multiple comparisons.
A nurse-led, multicomponent exercise intervention may have the potential to increase muscle strength and physical function in haemodialysis patients with possible or confirmed sarcopenia.

What problem did the study address? This study assessed the potential effects, safety, and feasibility of a nurse-led, multicomponent exercise intervention designed for haemodialysis patients with possible or confirmed sarcopenia. What were the main findings? A nurse-led exercise intervention appeared safe and feasible and may help to improve muscle strength and physical function in haemodialysis patients with possible or confirmed sarcopenia. However, future studies with larger sample sizes and longer follow-up periods are needed to assess the long-term effects. Where and on whom will the research have an impact? The results of this study may inform the development and future implementation of nurse-led exercise interventions for haemodialysis patients with sarcopenia.

Patients and family members were invited to collaborate with healthcare professionals in designing a nurse-led, multicomponent exercise intervention programme. Their contributions helped improve the feasibility and practicality of the exercise intervention.
The CONSORT 2025 checklist was used in the reporting of the study.
This trial was registered at www.chictr.org.cn (registration number: ChiCTR2200065863).

Article.ArticleTitle: The Effect of Implementing Orem's Self-Care Model on Balance and Fatigue in Patients With Diabetic Neuropathy: A Clinical Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: This study aims to determine the effect of applying Orem's self-care model on balance and fatigue in patients with diabetic neuropathy.
Randomized clinical trial.

Seventy diabetic neuropathy patients referred to Shahid Mofateh Clinic, affiliated with Yasuj University of Medical Sciences (YUMS), were chosen for this clinical trial study via convenience sampling and randomly assigned to an intervention group (n = 35) or a control group (n = 35). The intervention group received care based on Orem's self-care model from a graduate nursing student over 2 months, followed by 1 month of self-care at home. The control group received no intervention. Both groups completed the research questionnaires (the Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory and the Berg Balance Test) at pretest and posttest. Data were analysed in SPSS version 27 using an ANCOVA test.

Before the intervention, there were no significant between-group differences (p > 0.05). After the intervention, fatigue was significantly lower in the intervention group, with an adjusted mean difference of -9.40 points (95% CI: -11.09 to -7.71; p < 0.001; partial η2 = 0.647). Balance scores were significantly higher in the intervention group across low, mean, and high baseline levels, with adjusted mean differences of 7.01, 5.77, and 4.52 points, respectively (all p < 0.001). The group × baseline balance interaction was significant (F(1,66) = 5.69, p = 0.020; partial η2 = 0.079).
Nurses are recommended to apply Orem's self-care model as an effective structured intervention to reduce fatigue and improve balance in patients with diabetic neuropathy.

Patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathy (diagnosed by an internist using TCSS) who participated in this randomized clinical trial evaluating Orem's self-care model effects on balance and fatigue.

Article.ArticleTitle: Effect of Food on the Pharmacokinetics, Pharmacodynamics, and Safety of Zastaprazan, a Potassium-Competitive Acid Blocker, in Healthy Participants.

Abstract.AbstractText: Zastaprazan (JP-1366) is a novel potassium-competitive acid blocker characterized by rapid onset and sustained acid suppression. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of food on the pharmacokinetics (PK), pharmacodynamics (PD), and safety of zastaprazan in healthy participants. In this randomized, open-label, two-period crossover phase 1 study, 24 healthy participants received a single oral dose of zastaprazan 20 mg under fasted and fed conditions. PK parameters were evaluated using noncompartmental analysis, and PD effects were assessed through continuous intragastric pH monitoring. Under fed conditions, peak exposure (Cmax) decreased (geometric mean ratio [GMR], 0.6997; 90% confidence interval [CI], 0.6292-0.7781), whereas systemic exposure (AUClast) increased (GMR, 1.3783; 90% CI, 1.2688-1.4973), accompanied by a delayed Tmax. Despite these PK differences, PD outcomes were comparable between fed and fasted conditions. The percentage of time with intragastric pH ≥ 4 over 24 h was similar under fed and fasted conditions (70.01% vs. 69.19%), with no meaningful differences observed in other pH-based parameters. Zastaprazan was well tolerated, and no clinically significant safety concerns were identified. Food altered the rate and extent of zastaprazan absorption but did not affect its PD response. These findings indicate that food-related PK changes do not meaningfully affect PD outcomes and support the administration of zastaprazan without regard to meals. This flexibility may enhance its clinical utility as an acid-suppressive therapy. Trial Registration: The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05712681).

Article.ArticleTitle: Effects of psilocybin with psychological support on anhedonia in treatment-resistant depression: A randomized controlled pilot trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Anhedonia is a core feature of major depressive disorder (MDD) that is frequently resistant to available treatments. Psilocybin's specific efficacy for anhedonia remains unclear.
To evaluate psilocybin's efficacy for anhedonia in treatment-resistant MDD.

In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 20 participants with treatment-resistant MDD received psilocybin (25 mg or 1 mg) with psychological support. The primary outcome was change in the Dimensional Anhedonia Rating Scale (DARS) score at week 1; DARS change at week 8 was a secondary outcome. The Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale (SHAPS) and Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) were used as additional secondary outcome measures for anhedonia and overall depression severity, respectively.

The primary outcome was not statistically significant: between-group difference in DARS change at week 1 was 11.2 (95% confidence interval [CI], -1.0 to 23.3; p = 0.073). At week 8, the secondary DARS outcome indicated greater improvement in anhedonia with 25 mg (difference, 14.7; 95% CI, 2.5 to 26.8; p = 0.018). SHAPS improvement favored 25 mg at week 1 (difference, -3.2; 95% CI, -6.1 to -0.3; p = 0.029), but not week 8 (-2.1; 95% CI, -4.9 to 0.9; p = 0.168). MADRS improvement favored 25 mg at weeks 1 (-11.9; 95% CI, -19.2 to -4.5; p = 0.002) and 8 (-11.6; 95% CI, -19.0 to -4.2; p = 0.002).

Psilocybin 25 mg did not significantly improve anhedonia at the primary week 1 endpoint. However, improvements on secondary measures suggest potential benefits for anhedonia and depression severity that warrant confirmation in larger trials.

Article.ArticleTitle: Community health worker intervention to prevent incident type 2 diabetes: A cluster randomized trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) affects millions of Americans, and prediabetes significantly increases progression to T2DM. Community Health Workers (CHWs) may help prevent diabetes through behavioral interventions, but their effectiveness in real-world settings remains uncertain. We evaluated whether a CHW intervention prevents incident T2DM among adults with prediabetes.

Pragmatic, cluster-randomized controlled trial in primary care clinics at the Veterans Affairs NY Harbor Healthcare System (Manhattan) and Bellevue Hospital, New York City. The study included adults aged 18-75 years with HbA1c 5.7-6.4% and no prior diabetes or use of diabetes medications other than metformin. Primary care teams were cluster-randomized to a 12-month CHW program-health action plans, motivational interviewing, health education, and community referrals-versus usual care. The primary outcome was incident diabetes during up to 6 months' follow-up after the 12-month intervention. Secondary outcomes were changes in HbA1c, weight, blood pressure, lipids, and health care utilization.

Incident diabetes occurred in 5.9% of intervention patients versus 4.3% of controls (risk difference 1.6%; 95% CI -3.68% to 4.10%). No significant differences were observed in HbA1c, weight, blood pressure, or lipids. The intervention group had more primary care encounters (77.6% vs 62.5%) and emergency department encounters (35.0% vs 29.1%).

In this pragmatic trial, a 12-month CHW program did not reduce incident diabetes among adults with prediabetes but was associated with greater health care engagement (more primary care visits). More intensive or standardized CHW models should be tested to determine whether increased engagement translates into long-term metabolic benefit.
The study protocol was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03006666, 12/27/2016). https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03006666.

Article.ArticleTitle: Effects of a sleep program on sleep, performance and health in university students: Study protocol for a randomised controlled trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Insomnia and poor sleep are highly prevalent among university students and are linked to impaired mental and physical health, reduced cognitive functioning, and lower academic performance. Existing interventions for insomnia include cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), mindfulness, and sleep hygiene. CBT-I is widely recognised as effective but remains difficult to access for the general population and lack scalability, long-term follow-up, and feasibility in non-clinical settings. Pragmatic, group-based approaches that can be delivered within the university and are tailored to help students develop self-endorsed routines and competencies for better sleep, creating sustainable changes that extend beyond the program period, is needed.

This study is a pragmatic, two-arm randomised controlled trial evaluating the effectiveness of a group-based sleep program for university students with insomnia symptoms. A total of 118 full-time students aged 18-30 meeting diagnostic criteria for chronic insomnia disorder will be randomized (1:1) to either the intervention or a wait-list control group. The intervention comprises 12 weekly 90-minute group sessions followed by nine monthly follow-up meetings, facilitated by trained coaches. The program integrates core elements of CBT-I with motivational and coping strategies, delivered in an interactive and peer-supported format. The primary outcome is change in insomnia severity measured by the Bergen Insomnia Scale. Secondary outcomes include subjective and objective sleep measures, mental health, cognitive performance, academic attainment, health behaviours, physical fitness, and biological markers. Assessments will be conducted at baseline, post-program (12 weeks), and 12 months. A mixed methods process evaluation will assess fidelity, acceptability, mechanisms of impact, and contextual influences.

This trial will be among the first pragmatic evaluations of a structured, group-based sleep intervention tailored to university students with insomnia. Key strengths include the randomised controlled design, comprehensive outcome assessment, 12-month follow-up, and embedded process evaluation. If effective, the program could provide a feasible, scalable, and cost-effective model to improve sleep and therein health, and academic performance in young adults in higher education.

Article.ArticleTitle: The effect of acupuncture-rehabilitation therapy on brain functional plasticity in motor aphasia after ischemic stroke: a randomized clinical neuroimaging trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Motor aphasia is the most prevalent type of aphasia following ischemic stroke (IS). This study aims to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy and underlying neural mechanisms of acupuncture-rehabilitation (A-R) therapy on motor aphasia after IS. Twenty-six patients with post-IS motor aphasia were randomly assigned to either the A-R group or the Conventional Rehabilitation (CR) group in a 1:1 ratio, and matched by age and gender with 26 healthy controls (HCs). The CR group received standard treatment and language training, while the A-R group additionally underwent scalp acupoint cluster acupuncture. Behavioral assessments and Blood Oxygenation Level Dependent functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (BOLD-fMRI) scans were conducted before and after the four-week intervention to evaluate therapeutic outcomes and underlying mechanisms. Compared to HCs, patients exhibited decreased Amplitude of Low Frequency Fluctuations (ALFF) in the right precuneus (p < 0.05) and reduced Regional Homogeneity (ReHo) in the left precuneus/postcentral gyrus (p < 0.05). Enhanced functional connectivity (FC) was observed in regions including the left Broca's area and right superior temporal gyrus, left Broca's area and right inferior frontal orbitalis gyrus, left Broca's area and right precentral gyrus, left Broca's area and right postcentral gyrus (p < 0.05). After intervention, significant improvements were observed in Aphasia Quotient (AQ) scores and sub-item performance in both patient groups (p < 0.05), with the A-R group showing greater gains in AQ and spontaneous speech scores compared to the CR group (p < 0.05). FMRI results indicated a significant increase in mean ALFF (mALFF) in the left inferior temporal gyrus after A-R treatment (p < 0.05) compared to before, and higher szReHo in the left anterior central gyrus compared to the CR group (p < 0.05). FC between the left Broca's area and right precentral gyrus decreased in the A-R group (p < 0.05). Additionally, a negative correlation was observed between the right anterior central gyrus and listening comprehension (r = -0.574, p = 0.020). The findings suggest that both A-R and CR therapies enhance language function in patients with motor aphasia post-IS, with A-R therapy demonstrating superior efficacy. The therapeutic mechanism of A-R likely involves activating left hemisphere brain regions, suppressing right hemisphere activity, and restoring hemispheric balance to facilitate functional recovery.

Article.ArticleTitle: Auricular point acupressure for chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy: a randomized controlled trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) is common and persistent, with limited management options. This trial primarily examines whether auricular point acupressure (APA) improved CIPN outcomes versus usual care; a secondary pragmatic aim compared in-person mobile support (mAPA) with virtual (vAPA) delivery.

Two hundred twenty-seven cancer survivors with CIPN were randomized to mAPA (n = 80), vAPA (n = 75), or usual care (n = 72). Both APA arms received the same 4-week auricular point protocol; mAPA received in-person seed placement, and vAPA received video instruction for self-placement, with one coaching session for both. Usual care was standard oncologic and supportive care with no study-delivered APA. Primary outcome was a ≥20% reduction from baseline in an individualized composite outcome (ICO); each participant's highest-rated symptom-by-location item at baseline. Secondary outcomes were neuropathy interference, functional status, and quality of life. Intention-to-treat analyses used generalized estimating equations with multiple imputation and delta-adjusted sensitivity analyses.

At Week 1, both APA arms exceeded usual care (mAPA OR = 2.60, 95% CI 1.27-5.33; vAPA OR = 3.22; 95% CI 1.48-7.01; p < 0.01). The mAPA advantage persisted at Week 2 (OR = 2.49, p = 0.02). For neuropathy interference, mAPA benefits exceeded usual care every week (OR = 3.29-4.28, all p < 0.01). Among exploratory domains, anxiety, depression, and pain interference improved only in mAPA.

APA produced a short-lived advantage in CIPN severity and more consistent improvement in interference, specifically with in-person delivery. Findings are preliminary: no blinding or attention control, differential attrition (52% vAPA versus 96% usual care), and exploratory quality-of-life analyses.
ClinicalTrials.gov, ID NCT04920097 registered on 3 June 2021.

Article.ArticleTitle: Propofol versus remifentanil sedation for elective gastroscopy: a randomized controlled trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Propofol and remifentanil are widely used for elective gastroscopy sedation. The aim of this randomized controlled trial was to compare their safety profiles, patient-reported recovery quality, and endoscopist satisfaction.

This single-center randomized controlled trial enrolled 88 adults (American Society of Anesthesiologists I-III) undergoing elective gastroscopy, allocated 1:1 to propofol (Group P, n=44) or remifentanil (Group R, n=44). Sedation depth was standardized using the Bispectral Index (target 60-80) and Ramsay Sedation Scale (target 2-3). The primary outcome was the Quality of Recovery-15 score at 30 min post-procedure; secondary outcomes included complication incidence, awakening time, and endoscopist satisfaction.

Quality of Recovery-15 scores were comparable (median 140 vs. 140; median difference 0, 95%CI -1.0 to 1.0; p=0.95). Total complication incidence was 0% in Group P versus 61.4% in Group R (p<0.001), comprising bradycardia (27.3%), postoperative nausea and vomiting (20.5%), and desaturation (13.6%). Awakening time was shorter in Group R (3 vs. 60 s; p<0.001). Endoscopist satisfaction was significantly higher in Group P (90.9 vs. 56.8% excellent scores; p=0.003).

Despite comparable patient-reported recovery quality, propofol was associated with substantially fewer perioperative adverse events (0 vs. 61.4%) and higher endoscopist satisfaction, supporting its preferential use in routine elective gastroscopy sedation.
ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07336628. Registered January 2, 2026.

Article.ArticleTitle: Long-Term Marginal Bone Stability of BOPT Restorations on Bone-Level vs. Tissue-Level Implants: An 8-Year Prospective Clinical Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: The Biologically Oriented Preparation Technique (BOPT) has been applied to implant-supported restorations to promote peri-implant tissue stability. However, long-term evidence regarding marginal bone behavior remains limited. This study evaluated marginal bone loss after eight years of functional loading in bone-level and tissue-level implants restored according to the BOPT concept, as well as the influence of prosthesis type and arch location.

This prospective randomized clinical study included 122 posterior implants in 71 patients after eight years of follow-up: 57 bone-level implants and 65 tissue-level implants. All implants were restored with cement-retained metal-ceramic single crowns or fixed partial dentures. Marginal bone loss was assessed using standardized periapical radiographs obtained at prosthetic loading and after eight years. Generalized estimating equation models were used to account for multiple implants within the same patient.

Tissue-level implants showed significantly lower mesial marginal bone loss than bone-level implants (0.49 ± 0.77 mm versus 0.78 ± 0.93 mm; p = 0.031). No significant differences were observed for distal or mean marginal bone loss. Fixed partial dentures were associated with greater mesial bone loss than single crowns (p = 0.025), whereas arch location did not significantly affect bone remodeling (p = 0.838).

Both implant systems demonstrated limited long-term marginal bone remodeling. Nevertheless, the significant difference was restricted to the mesial aspect, and the findings cannot be attributed exclusively to implant placement level or to the BOPT concept because the two implant systems differed in macrogeometry, surface characteristics and transmucosal configuration.

Tissue-level implants showed lower mesial marginal bone loss after eight years, whereas distal and mean marginal bone loss did not differ significantly between systems. These findings should be interpreted considering the differences between the implant systems and the limitations of two-dimensional radiographic assessment.

Article.ArticleTitle: Efficacy of Stellate Ganglion Block for Preventing Postoperative Atrial Fibrillation After Cardiac Surgery: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Stellate ganglion block (SGB) may reduce postoperative atrial fibrillation (POAF) by modulating the autonomic nervous system. This study evaluated the efficacy of preoperative SGB in preventing POAF following cardiac surgery.

In this single-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 140 patients undergoing valve surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass were assigned (1:1) to ultrasound-guided right SGB with 7 mL of 0.5% ropivacaine or 7 mL of normal saline. The primary outcome was the incidence of POAF from postoperative day 0 to day 7 or until discharge.

A total of 132 patients completed the study and were included in the modified intention-to-treat population (SGB group: n=65; saline group: n=67). POAF occurred in 43% of the SGB group and 40% of the saline group (odds ratio [OR], 0.99 [95% CI, 0.46-2.15], adjusted P=0.989). The SGB group demonstrated a lower incidence of intraoperative ventricular fibrillation/ventricular tachycardia requiring defibrillation after aortic cross-clamp release (6% versus 19%; OR, 0.21 [95% CI, 0.06-0.80]; adjusted P=0.022), lower postoperative high-sensitivity troponin I levels (median difference: -2562 ng/L [95% CI, -4301 to -45]; P=0.045), and a reduced risk of postoperative acute kidney injury (5% versus 18%; OR, 0.24 [95% CI, 0.06-0.98]; adjusted P=0.046).

While preoperative SGB did not reduce the incidence of POAF, it was associated with potential benefits, including a lower requirement for intraoperative defibrillation attributable to ventricular arrhythmias, attenuated myocardial injury (as indicated by lower high-sensitivity troponin I levels), and a decreased risk of postoperative acute kidney injury.

Article.ArticleTitle: Tezepelumab in Canadian Adults With Severe Chronic Rhinosinusitis With Nasal Polyps: A Subgroup Analysis of the Phase 3 WAYPOINT Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Tezepelumab, a monoclonal antibody targeted against thymic stromal lymphopoietin, was recently approved in Canada for the treatment of severe uncontrolled chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP). Its effectiveness specifically in the Canadian setting has not been evaluated.
To analyze the efficacy and safety of tezepelumab in Canadian patients enrolled in the WAYPOINT trial and contextualize the findings with respect to the Canadian healthcare environment.
Post hoc analysis of a multinational, parallel-group, randomized, placebo-controlled, Phase 3 trial.
Forty-nine Canadian adult patients with severe uncontrolled CRSwNP.
Subgroup of Canadian patients enrolled in the WAYPOINT trial.
Tezepelumab 210 mg (n = 25) or placebo (n = 24) administered subcutaneously every 4 weeks for 52 weeks.
The co-primary endpoints were change from baseline to week 52 in endoscopic total nasal polyp score (NPS) and patient-reported bi-weekly nasal congestion score (NCS).

The Canadian cohort had higher numbers of patients with asthma and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug-exacerbated respiratory disease than in the full study population. Objective and subjective signs and symptoms of CRSwNP were significantly improved with tezepelumab compared with placebo in the Canadian cohort, including both co-primary endpoints (least squares mean difference vs placebo [95% confidence interval]: total NPS, -2.53 [-3.33 to -1.73], P < .0001; mean NCS, -1.10 [-1.62 to -0.58], P < .0001) and all secondary efficacy endpoints in the overall population. The magnitude of clinical benefit was similar in the Canadian cohort versus the full study population, with less frequent use of rescue therapy (nasal polyp surgery and/or systemic corticosteroids) compared to placebo. The safety profile of tezepelumab was consistent in the Canadian cohort as in the full study population. There were no serious adverse events (AEs) or discontinuations due to AEs in the Canadian cohort.
Tezepelumab is an effective and safe treatment for severe uncontrolled CRSwNP in a patient population that is reflective of the Canadian clinical landscape.
The multinational WAYPOINT trial findings are relevant to patients with CRSwNP routinely seen in Canadian clinical practice, supporting their applicability in the Canadian healthcare context.

Article.ArticleTitle: Study Protocol: Efficacy of Jintiange Capsule in Lumbar Disc Herniation: A Single-Center, Randomized Controlled Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Lumbar disc herniation (LDH) is a leading cause of chronic low back pain (LBP), severely impairing patients' quality of life and imposing a substantial global socioeconomic burden. Conservative treatment remains the first-line clinical option, but the commonly prescribed drug celecoxib carries a risk of gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation. Traditional Chinese medicine preparations have been proposed as alternatives, although current evidence is insufficient. Jintiange (JTG) capsule, developed as a substitute for tiger bone, exerts its pharmacological effects by inhibiting osteoclastogenesis and regulating the NF-κB pathway. Previous studies have identified a close association between the p38MAPK/NF-κB pathway and pain induced by LDH. However, the efficacy of JTG in treating LDH remains unclear. High-quality research is thus urgently needed to provide evidence-based support for its clinical application.

This randomized, single-center clinical trial will enroll 68 participants, centrally allocated 1:1 to receive either JTG capsules plus comprehensive Western medicine (celecoxib + eperisone) or Western medicine alone. All participants will complete an 8-week treatment phase (celecoxib for 2 weeks + eperisone for 8 weeks; with JTG capsules added for 8 weeks in the experimental group), with a follow-up at Week 12 (4 weeks after treatment completion). The primary outcome is the change in the Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA) score for LBP, a validated instrument for evaluating treatment efficacy in LDH. Secondary outcomes include the Patient Global Impression of Change (PGIC), Visual Analog Scale (VAS) score, SF-12 quality-of-life score, and elastic modulus of the lumbar muscles. Safety monitoring and adverse-event recording will occur throughout the study. The primary endpoint will be analyzed using the analysis of covariance. Longitudinal VAS scores at Weeks 2, 8, and 12 will be analyzed using a mixed model for repeated measures. PGIC will be analyzed as an ordinal categorical outcome, while other secondary outcomes will be analyzed using appropriate parametric or nonparametric methods. All analyses will be performed using SPSS 28.0, with no interim analysis planned.

This trial will evaluate the clinical efficacy of JTG capsules combined with Western medicine for LBP and will explore its safety profile as a secondary/exploratory endpoint. Given the open-label combination design, safety findings will be interpreted with caution, and causality attribution to JTG alone will be limited. The findings are expected to provide an evidence-based treatment option, supporting the potential role of Chinese patent medicine in LBP management.
Chinese Registry of Clinical Trials: ChiCTR2300069735.

Article.ArticleTitle: A multicenter, randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, positive-controlled study of the general treatment method using Tanreqing capsule in uncomplicated influenza.

Abstract.AbstractText: To investigate the effects of the method of clearing heat, resolving phlegm, and detoxification, represented by Tanreqing capsule (TRQC, ), on influenza.

A total of 122 patients with uncomplicated influenza in the Beijing-Tianjin area were randomly divided into an observation group and a control group. They were treated with TRQC plus oseltamivir placebo or oseltamivir plus TRQC placebo for 5 d, respectively. The relief time for influenza symptoms, individual symptom relief time, the frequency of antipyretic drug usage, and the frequency of antibiotic drug usage were analyzed.

External wind-cold syndrome (28.69%) and external wind-heat syndrome (45.08%) were the most common syndrome types. The number of patients in TRQC group achieved normal temperature within 1 d was significantly more than oseltamivir group (72.88% vs50.80%, P < 0.05). There were no significant differences in the time for influenza symptom relief and individual symptom relief between the two groups. TRQC showed a better heat relief effect than oseltamivir on the fifth day of treatment.

TRQC, as a "Tongzhi" method (General treatment), has a curative effect on uncomplicated influenza that is similar to oseltamivir, with a better effect on prolonged fever. TRQC is an effective method of general treatment for influenza and can serve as an alternative therapy for managing large-scale influenza epidemics.

Journal.Title: Journal of traditional Chinese medicine = Chung i tsa chih ying wen pan

Article.ArticleTitle: Bufei Huoxue capsules enhance lung function in pneumoconiosis: a multicenter, randomized clinical trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: To clarify the efficacy and safety of Bufei Huoxue (BFHX) capsules for the treatment of pneumoconiosis.

This multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial enrolled patients with pneum-oconiosis from five centers between June 2020 and June 2023. Participants were randomized 1∶1 to receive oral BFHX capsules or matched placebo (4 capsules, thrice daily) for 24 weeks. The primary endpoint was the change from baseline in forced vital capacity percent predicted (FVC%) at 24 weeks. Secondary outcomes included changes in forced expiratory volume in 1 s percent predicted (FEV1%), 6-min walk test (6MWT) distance, COPD assessment test (CAT) score, Modified British Medical Research Council (mMRC) dyspnea scale score, and serum biomarkers at weeks 8 and 24. Safety was assessed through adverse events and laboratory analyses. Efficacy was evaluated in both the full analysis set (FAS) and per-protocol set (PPS), with blinding maintained throughout the trial.

In total, 162 patients were included in the study. For the primary outcome, the change from baseline in FVC% at 24 weeks was significantly greater in BFHX group than placebo group [BFHX-placebo least squares (LS): 5.65 ± 2.01, 95% confidence interval (CI) (1.68, 9.62), P = 0.0056]. A significant difference of FVC% was also observed at week 8 [BFHX-placebo LS: 3.50 ± 1.72, 95% CI(0.11, 6.90), P = 0.0434]. Significant improvements in secondary outcomes were also observed at week 24, including FEV1% [BFHX-placebo LS: 5.33 ± 2.51, 95% CI(0.37, 10.3), P = 0.0352], 6MWT distance [BFHX-placebo LS: 22.7 ± 8.76, 95% CI(5.40, 40.1), P = 0.0105], CAT score [BFHX-placebo LS: －2.14 ± 0.85, 95% CI(－3.82, －0.46), P = 0.0130], and mMRC score [BFHX-placebo LS: －0.34 ± 0.10, 95% CI(－0.54, －0.13), P = 0.0014]. The mMRC score also showed improvement at week 8 [BFHX-placebo LS: －0.25 ± 0.11, 95% CI(－0.47, －0.02), P = 0.0308]. Results were consistent in both the per-protocol and full analysis sets. No significant between-group differences were observed in laboratory safety parameters, inflammatory markers, or coagulation profiles (all P > 0.05). The overall safety profile was similar between the two groups.

BFHX capsules improved lung function, exercise tolerance, and respiratory symptoms in patients with pneumoconiosis. Therefore, this treatment can be safely and effectively used in patients with pneumoconiosis.

Journal.Title: Clinical implant dentistry and related research

Article.ArticleTitle: Treatment of Small Peri-Implant Buccal Dehiscence Defects With SCTG or GBR: 3-Year Results of a Pilot Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: To evaluate and compare subepithelial connective tissue grafts (SCTG) and guided bone regeneration (GBR) for the treatment of small peri-implant buccal bone dehiscences over a 3-year follow-up, in terms of profilometric contour change, peri-implant parameters and patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs).

Patients presenting with small buccal bone dehiscences (≤ 3 mm) after single implant placement were included. Defect sites were randomly treated with either SCTG or GBR, while five patients without dehiscences served as a negative control group. All patients received an implant crown and were followed for 3 years. Profilometric measurements, marginal bone levels, peri-implant parameters, and PROMs were recorded at baseline, 1, and 3 years. Data were analyzed descriptively.

A total of 16 patients were available for the 3-year follow-up (SCTG, n = 5; GBR, n = 6; negative control, n = 5). Both augmentation approaches maintained stable buccal soft-tissue contours. At 1 mm below the mucosal margin, the median buccal contour change was 0.19 mm (Q1: -0.28; Q3: 0.29) in the SCTG group and 0.11 mm (Q1: -0.20; Q3: 0.30) in the GBR group. At 3 mm below the mucosal margin, the corresponding median contour changes were 0.05 mm (Q1: -0.36; Q3: 0.31) for SCTG and -0.05 mm (Q1: -0.22; Q3: 0.07) for GBR. Peri-implant clinical parameters (probing depth, bleeding on probing, and plaque) remained stable, indicating maintained peri-implant health in both groups. Marginal bone levels were preserved throughout the observation period and oral health-related quality of life remained high and comparable between the SCTG and GBR groups.

Within the limitations of this pilot study, both SCTG and GBR were associated with stable buccal contour conditions and favorable peri-implant health over a 3-year follow-up period. These findings were observed under adequate self-performed plaque control and adherence to supportive care. Adequately powered RCTs are needed to confirm these findings.

Article.ArticleTitle: Classical popliteal sciatic block versus Crosswise Approach to Popliteal Sciatic (CAPS) block for below-knee surgery: a randomised controlled trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Ultrasound-guided popliteal sciatic nerve block is frequently used for below-knee surgery. The classical approach often requires lateral decubitus or prone positioning, which may be uncomfortable for patients with lower limb injuries. The Crosswise Approach to Popliteal Sciatic (CAPS) block allows the procedure to be performed with the patient supine. This randomised trial compared the classical approach with CAPS in terms of patient comfort, block performance, and clinical outcomes.

Eighty American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status I-III patients undergoing unilateral below-knee surgery were randomised to receive either a classical popliteal sciatic block in the lateral position (Group A) or a CAPS block in the supine position (Group B). All procedures were ultrasound-guided with 20 mL of 0.5% ropivacaine after lignocaine skin infiltration. All patients also received a femoral nerve block. Pain scores (verbal numerical rating scale [VNRS]) during positioning and block performance, fentanyl requirements, block performance time, sensory onset time, block success, adverse effects, and patient satisfaction were assessed.

All blocks were successful. Median highest pain scores were low in both groups (1.5 [classical] vs. 3.0 [CAPS] VNRS; p = 0.050). The proportion of patients reporting no pain (VNRS = 0) did not differ significantly between groups (30.0% [classical] vs. 15.0% [CAPS]; p = 0.180). Fentanyl supplementation (any dose) was required in 45% of Group A and 60% of Group B (p = 0.365). Block performance time was shorter with CAPS (10.5 min) than the classical approach (12.0 min; p = 0.002). Sensory onset time was similar (~ 20 min; p = 0.919). No major complications occurred. Transient sensory symptoms lasting more than 24 h occurred in two patients (5.0%) in Group A and one (2.5%) in Group B. Patient satisfaction remained high in both groups, with 75.0% of Group A and 67.5% of Group B rating satisfaction as 4 or 5 on a 5-point Likert scale (p = 0.120).

Both techniques provide effective and safe anaesthesia for below-knee surgery with comparable clinical outcomes. CAPS provides a logistical advantage by allowing the procedure to be performed in the supine position, which may be of value in patients unable to tolerate lateral decubitus positioning, as well as a modest reduction in procedural time (approximately 1.5 min). Either technique may be selected based on patient factors and operator preference.

Article.ArticleTitle: Chlorhexidine within a standardized oral-care bundle for the prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia: a pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover trial in six medical intensive care units.

Abstract.AbstractText: Chlorhexidine (CHX) has been a long-standing component of oral-care bundles for preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), but recent evidence has questioned its benefit in non-cardiac-surgery ICU. We evaluated whether adding 0.12% CHX to standardized oral-care bundle provides incremental benefit in a mixed medical ICU.

We conducted a prospective, pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover (AB/BA) trial in six adult medical ICUs of a single tertiary-care academic hospital in Bhubaneswar, India. ICUs were randomized as three ICUs of two Period of 9 months with the multicomponent oral-care bundle without chlorhexidine and three with the same bundle plus 0.12% chlorhexidine with a 1-month wash-in and re-training interval. Consecutive adults ventilated for ≥ 48 h were included. The primary outcome was VAP incidence density (Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score (CPIS) > 6) as per 1,000 ventilator-days. Secondary outcomes were 28-day all-cause mortality, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU length of stay, 28- day ventilator-free days, Beck Oral Assessment Scale (BOAS) and Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT) scores. The primary model was a population-averaged Poisson generalized estimating equation (GEE) and adjustment for treatment, period, sequence, age, sex, APACHE II, and SOFA.

A total of 1,035 patients (637 No CHX, 398 CHX) accrued 10,024 ventilator-days (5,918 vs. 4,106). Groups were well balanced at baseline (mean age ≈ 55 years; APACHE II ≈ 19.6; SOFA ≈ 13.4). VAP occurred in 100/5,918 ventilator-days (16.9 per 1,000) vs. 77/4,106 (18.8 per 1,000) (No CHX vs. CHX). The adjusted Poisson incidence rate ratio was 1.08 (95% CI 0.84-1.38; p = 0.56). 28-day mortality was 28.7% vs. 26.4% (no CHX vs. CHX) (adjusted OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.65-1.15; p = 0.33). ICU length of stay was longer in the CHX arm (adjusted mean difference + 0.89 days, 95% CI + 0.19 to + 1.58; p = 0.013). BOAS and CPOT scores did not differ.

In this trial, adding 0.12% chlorhexidine to a standardized oral-care bundle did not reduce VAP incidence density or 28-day mortality and was associated with a modest increase in ICU length of stay. Routine CHX use provided no clear incremental benefit in a mixed medical ICU population.

Article.ArticleTitle: Improvement in naming with tDCS and alteration of functional connectivity in post-stroke aphasia: a randomized controlled trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: This study aimed to investigate the effects of anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (A-tDCS) over the left Sylvian parietal temporal region (SPT) on picture naming and auditory comprehension, as well as changes in brain functional connectivity in post-stroke aphasic patients.

This is a double-blind, sham-controlled, randomized controlled study. Sixty aphasic patients were randomly assigned to receive either active or sham tDCS over the SPT as well as speech-language therapy for four weeks. Standardized aphasia assessments and electroencephalogram (EEG) examinations were conducted before and after the treatment. The EEG nonlinear index of cross approximate entropy (C-ApEn) was used to assess brain functional connectivity.

The tDCS group demonstrated significantly greater improvements than the control group in both picture naming and auditory word-picture identification scores (p < 0.001). Regression analysis revealed that the group (tDCS/control) was the primary factor associated with improving picture naming. The functional connectivity of F3-P3, F7-P3, T3-T5, T5-P3, T5-C3, T4-T6, T3-T4, and T5-T6 significantly increased following tDCS.

Anodal tDCS over the left SPT can improve picture naming and auditory comprehension in subacute post-stroke aphasia. Potential mechanisms include enhanced connectivity within the left-hemisphere dorsal/ventral streams, the executive control network, and between the bilateral temporal lobes. These functional connectivity changes provide neural evidence for the effect of tDCS on naming improvement. Clinical trial registry number ChiCTR-TRC-14005072.

Article.ArticleTitle: Development, implementation, and evaluation of a belief-targeted non-face-to-face leisure-time physical activity promotion program for South Korean University students.

Abstract.AbstractText: Despite a sharp decline in physical activity levels among university students since the COVID-19 pandemic, physical activity programs for this population remain limited. Our previous research examined key beliefs influencing physical activity behavior among university students at a Korean university during the COVID-19 pandemic. Accordingly, this study aimed to develop, implement, and evaluate a non-face-to-face leisure-time physical activity (NFTF-LTPA) promotion program for university students, focusing on three beliefs-health, friends, and laziness-identified as key determinants of physical activity behavior in our previous study.

Undergraduate students were newly recruited from the same university and departments (i.e., the College of Social Sciences and the School of Business) as our prior study. Participants were stratified and randomly assigned to intervention or control groups and a belief-targeted intervention was implemented for three months. Process evaluations were conducted at mid-, and post-intervention, and outcomes were assessed at pre-, mid-, and post-intervention. A one-month follow-up survey was also conducted after the intervention ended. A 2 × 4 repeated measures generalized linear model was conducted and subgroup analyses examined participants with high intervention adherence (PHIA) compared with controls.

Among the total analytic sample, significant group × time interaction effects at the α = 0.10 level were observed for outcome evaluation of behavioral beliefs (F = 2.70; p = 0.072; [Formula: see text]= 0.05) and motivation to comply with normative beliefs (F = 2.54; p = 0.085; [Formula: see text]= 0.05). However, no significant group × time interaction effects were observed for control beliefs, intention, or LTPA participation. In an exploratory subgroup analysis, a significant group × time interaction effect was observed for the control belief of laziness (F = 3.85; p = 0.031; [Formula: see text] = 0.18). Post hoc analyses indicated lower perceived laziness at the program midpoint in the PHIA group compared with the control group.

Although the intervention produced changes in selected belief components among the total analytic sample, these changes did not translate into significant improvements in intention or behavior. Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested potential changes in control beliefs among participants with higher intervention adherence. These findings provide preliminary insights into the development, implementation, and evaluation of belief-targeted NFTF-LTPA promotion programs for university students.
The trial was retrospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT07423403; 19 February 2026).

Article.ArticleTitle: The relationship between in-socket mechanics and patient-reported comfort and function, a randomized crossover trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Lower limb loss presents significant challenges, resulting in chronic health issues and impacting the quality of life. Prosthetic socket design is crucial for optimizing comfort and function in individuals with limb loss.

This study aimed to determine the relationship between in-socket mechanics and patient-reported comfort and function, hypothesizing that residual femur motion, skin strain, and pressure distribution correlate with these outcomes. Ten individuals with transfemoral limb loss participated, with modifications made to personalized prosthetic check sockets to assess these variables, and data from eight subjects were included in the analysis. Data collection included CT scans, dynamic biplane radiography, in-socket pressure measurements, plantar pressure assessments, ground reaction force analyses, conventional motion capture assessments, and patient-reported outcomes. Generalized estimated equations were used to examine the relationships between peak skin strain during gait and patient reported outcomes and correlation matrices were constructed to explore relationships between static imaging, skin strain, residual bone motion, and gait kinematics.

Our findings indicate that the combination of skin strain metrics significantly predicts variability in comfort, while the overall model was not significant with respect to function. Significant correlations were also observed between static imaging and dynamic residual bone motion.

These results suggest that minimizing and monitoring skin strain, particularly in the anterior central socket region, can enhance prosthetic fit and patient satisfaction. Additionally, static imaging under different loads effectively predicts dynamic displacements, offering a less invasive method for clinical assessments. These insights highlight the need for integrating objective in-socket measurements into clinical practice to improve prosthetic socket fitting, ultimately enhancing the quality of life for individuals with lower limb loss.

Article.ArticleTitle: Effect of motivational interviews and peer education on adherence to pre-exposure prophylaxis among key populations in Kisangani: a randomized clinical trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: The present study aimed to evaluate the effect of motivational interviews and peer education on adherence to pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) among key populations in Kisangani.

This study utilizes a randomized controlled trial design to assess the effect of motivational interviewing and peer education on adherence to PrEP among key populations in Kisangani, DRC. The trial was conducted over 12 months, with data collection points at baseline and each month. In total, 141 participants agreed to participate in the study, and after evaluating the eligibility criteria, 126 met the criteria and were randomly assigned to the two study groups. Intervention group: Participants received monthly adherence counseling on PrEP, and motivational interviews with healthcare providers at the friendly centers. Peer educators also sensitized them on PrEP adherence within their residential and social environments.

Participants were monitored on PrEP according to routine procedures at the friendly centers. Participants were randomly assigned to either the intervention or control group based on their order of enrollment. Data were collected at the friendly centers for key populations at enrollment visits and, during follow-up visits. Survival analysis was performed using Kaplan-Meier survival curves, and survival curves were compared using the Log-Rank test. Hazard ratios (HR) derived from the Cox model and their confidence intervals were presented.

We found that in the intervention group, 52 participants (82.5%) adhered to PrEP over the twelve months, compared to 16 participants (25.3%) in the control group (p < 0.0001). Without intervention, the risk of non-adherence was five times higher in the control group (HR 4.9, 95%CI [1.6937-14.2823], p = 0.003). Factors that strengthened adherence to PrEP included attending appointments for ARV refills (HR 0.15, 95% CI [0.0720-0.3404], p < 0.0001) and having adherence support (HR 0.26, 95% CI [0.1280-0.5482], p < 0.0001).

Although the data confirm higher adherence in the intervention group, the high HIV incidence rate in the control group can be explained not only by the absence of the intervention but also by other factors related to the participants' lives that may have contributed to the higher seroconversion rate compared to the intervention group.

Article.ArticleTitle: Combined regional anesthesia versus general anesthesia for elective shoulder arthroscopy: a prospective randomized trial of postoperative pain, with an exploratory cost analysis.

Abstract.AbstractText: Shoulder arthroscopy causes substantial postoperative pain and operating room resource use. Randomized trials integrating postoperative pain trajectory with sensitivity-tested cost analysis are limited. We compared combined three-block regional anesthesia with standard general anesthesia in elective shoulder arthroscopy.

In this prospective, randomized, parallel-group, single-center trial, 50 adults undergoing elective shoulder arthroscopy in the beach-chair position were allocated 1:1 to ultrasound-guided combined interscalene, supraclavicular, and superficial cervical plexus blocks with dexmedetomidine sedation or standard general anesthesia. The primary outcome was the resting Numeric Rating Scale (NRS, 0-10) pain score at 4 h. Pre-specified secondary outcomes included pain scores at the remaining timepoints, movement-evoked pain, patient and surgeon satisfaction, surgical duration, and intraoperative opioid consumption. Exploratory post-hoc outcomes included cumulative pain burden (area under the NRS-time curve), total perioperative cost, hemodynamic parameters, perioperative time components, rescue analgesia, postoperative nausea and vomiting, and complications.

Resting NRS at 4 h was lower with regional anesthesia than with general anesthesia (median 0 [IQR 0-0] vs. 4 [IQR 3-5]; Hodges-Lehmann median difference 4 points, 95% CI 3 to 4; p < 0.001) and remained lower through the 4-hour timepoint. Movement NRS increased at 12 and 24 h after block regression. Among the pre-specified secondary outcomes, patient and surgeon satisfaction was higher with regional anesthesia, while surgical duration was similar. In exploratory post-hoc analyses, the 24-hour cumulative pain burden was lower with regional anesthesia, total perioperative cost was approximately 38% lower with regional anesthesia across all sensitivity scenarios, total operating room time was shorter, and complication types differed qualitatively between groups with no significant difference in incidence detected.

Combined regional anesthesia provided superior early analgesia and greater patient and surgeon satisfaction than general anesthesia. Exploratory post-hoc analyses suggested lower 24-hour cumulative pain burden, lower total perioperative cost and shorter operating room utilization. These economic and operational findings should be considered hypothesis-generating.

Article.ArticleTitle: The effect of virtual reality glasses used during chest tube removal following open-heart surgery on pain and hemodynamic parameters: a randomized controlled trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Chest tube removal (CTR) following open-heart surgery is a painful procedure that may adversely affect patients' hemodynamic parameters.
This study aimed to determine the effect of virtual reality glasses (VRG) used during chest tube removal after open-heart surgery on pain levels and hemodynamic parameters.

This prospective, two-arm (1:1), randomized controlled trial included 82 patients undergoing open-heart surgery. Patients in the VRG group (n = 41) were exposed to relaxing forest-walk-themed virtual reality content starting five minutes before CTR and continuing for five minutes after the procedure. The control group (n = 41) received routine care without any additional intervention. Pain levels were assessed using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS), and hemodynamic parameters-systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), heart rate (HR), respiratory rate (RR), and peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO₂)-were recorded before CTR, immediately after, and at 5, 15, and 30 min post-procedure.

A significant group × time interaction was observed for pain (p = 0.003). After adjustment for baseline pain and multiple comparisons, pain was significantly lower in the VRG group than in the control group immediately after CTR (adjusted mean difference [VRG - Control]: -1.26, 95% CI: -1.85 to - 0.68; adjusted p < 0.001), whereas no significant between-group differences were observed at 5, 15, or 30 min. A significant group × time interaction was also observed for SpO₂ (p < 0.001), with significantly higher SpO₂ in the VRG group immediately after CTR (adjusted mean difference: 2.70, 95% CI: 1.88 to 3.53; adjusted p < 0.001). No significant group × time interactions were observed for SBP, DBP, HR, or RR.

VRG use during CTR was associated with lower pain immediately after the procedure and higher SpO₂ immediately after CTR. No significant effects were observed for SBP, DBP, HR, or RR. These findings suggest that VRG may be a useful non-pharmacological adjunct for short-term pain management during CTR following open-heart surgery. Further studies are needed to confirm its effects on oxygenation and other hemodynamic parameters.
ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05585853) first submitted on October 12, 2022, and first posted on October 19, 2022.

Article.ArticleTitle: A creative dance-supported CO-OP intervention for older adults with mild cognitive impairment: an assessor-blinded, external pilot randomised controlled trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: In mild cognitive impairment (MCI) a clinical syndrome associated with, but not an inevitable consequence of, ageing deficits in executive function and cognitive-motor integration can compromise everyday functioning. Few rehabilitation programmes combine occupation-centred strategy training with cognitively demanding movement. This external pilot trial aimed to assess feasibility and generate preliminary effect estimates for adding graded creative dance to a Cognitive Orientation to daily Occupational Performance (CO-OP) programme in older adults with MCI.

Assessor-blinded external pilot randomised controlled trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06644690). Twenty-six community-dwelling adults with MCI were randomised to CO-OP plus creative dance or CO-OP alone (n = 13 per group). CO-OP comprised 24 individual sessions over 8 weeks; the experimental arm added 20-25 min of graded creative dance per session, with total session duration and therapist contact time matched across groups. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, post-intervention (8 weeks), and 3- and 6-month follow-up. The prespecified primary outcome was executive function (Trail Making Test Part B [TMT-B] completion time); secondary outcomes included global cognition (Montreal Cognitive Assessment [MoCA]), visual memory (Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure Test [RCFT]), dual-task cognitive errors, and depressive symptoms and loneliness. Analyses used linear mixed-effects models and generalised estimating equations, with an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis.

Follow-up data were available for 23 participants (88% retention). No intervention-related adverse events occurred; one unrelated serious adverse event (hip fracture from a fall at home) was recorded. For the prespecified primary outcome (executive function, TMT-B), the combined programme showed no between-group advantage. In exploratory secondary analyses, global cognition (MoCA) favoured the combined programme at all post-intervention timepoints in completer analyses (large effect sizes) and after covariate adjustment (baseline score, age and sex) but was attenuated and non-significant under intention-to-treat analysis. Dual-task cognitive errors showed a significant group-by-time interaction, reflecting differing between-group trajectories. These secondary findings are hypothesis-generating.

This external pilot showed no superiority of CO-OP plus creative dance over CO-OP alone for the prespecified primary outcome (executive function). Preliminary signals for global cognition and dual-task accuracy warrant confirmation in an adequately powered definitive trial with a prespecified, clinically meaningful primary endpoint.

Article.ArticleTitle: First-in-Human Phase 1b/2a Trial Shows Safety with MEK 1/2 Inhibitor EDV2209 as A Novel Treatment for Spontaneous Subarachnoid Hemorrhage.

Abstract.AbstractText: We report findings from a Phase 1/2a clinical trial (EUCT No. 2024-514590-22-00, STOP-DCI), an interventional, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multiple ascending-dose, first-in-human trial to determine safety and evaluate clinical outcome for the MEK 1/2 inhibitor EDV2209 in patients with severe spontaneous subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). In Phase 1b (N = 11), three cohorts received a single intracerebral ventricular (ICV) bolus (8.55 µg, 17-28.5 µg). In Phase 2a (N = 16), two cohorts were given three ICV injections of 28.5 µg EDV2209 or placebo over 18 h, beginning within 8 h of SAH onset.The study found an equal distribution of adverse events between treatment and placebo with no treatment-associated safety concerns. Outcomes and mortality were as expected or better for patients with severe SAH in the patients treated with EDV2209. Pharmacokinetics were reproducibly stable in the CSF with no detectable levels of EDV2209 in plasma.Treatment with EDV2209 was considered safe and was interpreted to provide potential benefit for improving patient outcome following severe SAH. These results provide a rationale to continue with a Phase 2b / 3 study powered to determine efficacy as well as safety.

Article.ArticleTitle: Limosilactobacillus reuteri for oral mucositis in patients undergoing radiotherapy for malignant head and neck tumors: a randomized controlled trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Oral mucositis (OM) is a major toxicity in patients with head and neck cancer undergoing radiotherapy. Here we conducted a double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized phase II trial (NCT06285591) from March 2024 to January 2025 at West China Hospital of Sichuan University to evaluate whether Limosilactobacillus reuteri (L. reuteri) supplementation could reduce severe OM (SOM; WHO Oral Toxicity criteria grade ≥3). A total of 160 patients were randomly assigned to receive L. reuteri probiotic lozenges or placebo twice daily during radiotherapy. The primary endpoint was the incidence of SOM, and secondary endpoints included SOM onset and duration, as well as the incidence, onset, and duration of any-grade OM. Safety outcomes were monitored throughout the study. The primary endpoint was met, with a lower incidence of SOM in the L. reuteri group than in the placebo group (37.5% vs 61.3%; relative risk 0.61; 95% confidence interval 0.44-0.85; absolute risk reduction 23.8 percentage points, 95% CI 8.7% to 38.8%; P = 0.004). L. reuteri supplementation also delayed SOM onset and shortened SOM duration. No significant safety concerns were observed. These findings indicate that L. reuteri supplementation reduces SOM incidence and severity in patients with head and neck cancer receiving radiotherapy.

Article.ArticleTitle: Identification of functional bacterial-viral pneumotypes associated with airway inflammation and all-cause mortality in critically ill patients.

Abstract.AbstractText: Alterations in lung virome and bacteriome compositions have been associated with hospital-acquired pneumonia in critically ill patients, but data on lung microbiome functions underlying progression to severe complications remain unclear. Here, we analyse 184 endotracheal aspirates (ETAs) collected in 94 intubated critically ill patients enrolled in a clinical trial (NCT04793568). Combining viral-metagenomics with metatranscriptomics analyses, we identify a high-risk functional pneumotype observed before the onset of hospital-acquired pneumonia and associated with lung inflammation and mortality. This unfavourable pneumotype is characterised by enrichment in virulent Streptococcus-bacteriophages and temperate Klebsiella-bacteriophages, decreased transcriptional activity of commensal taxa such as Streptococcus and Alloprevotella, and increased transcriptional activity of Klebsiella pneumoniae. Machine-learning models define two-viral- and four-bacterial-factor signatures predicting unfavourable pneumotype (AUC 0.8 and 0.7, respectively). Validation in an independent cohort (NCT02003196) of 117 ICU patients (239 ETAs) demonstrates the robustness of the association of these signatures with the risk of mortality. Causal inference identifies virulent bacteriophages associated with Streptococcus and host genes including IL18R1, ADM and PTX3, as key regulators of severe lung dysbiosis linked to mortality in critically ill patients.

Article.ArticleTitle: Different concentrations of atropine in children with high myopia: a 2-year multicenter double-blind, randomized controlled trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: High myopia in children risks irreversible visual impairment, yet optimal interventions remain debated. This multicenter double-blind, randomized-controlled trial aims to evaluate the effect and safety of different atropine eyedrops for myopia control in children with high myopia, conducted in Shanghai Eye Diseases Prevention and Treatment Center, Shanghai General Hospital and Shanghai Ninth People's Hospital. Recruitment started on July 4th, 2021 and final follow-up was August, 21st, 2024. 219 children aged 6-12 years with myopia of at least -5.0 diopter (D) were recruited and randomly assigned to use either 0.01%(N = 76), 0.04%(N = 72), or 0.10%(N = 71) atropine eyedrops once nightly for both eyes over 24 months, and 182 participants completed trial; 219 (76:72:71) randomized cases were analyzed. Main outcome was cycloplegic spherical equivalent (SE) change from baseline over 24 months. After 24 months, mean SE progression was -0.92 D, -0.78 D and -0.56 D for 0.01%, 0.04% and 0.10% atropine, respectively. The 0.10% atropine significantly reduced myopia progression by 0.35 D (95%CI: 0.12 D, 0.58 D) versus 0.01%, while 0.04% atropine did not show significant difference; however, at 12 months, both higher concentrations demonstrated significantly greater reductions (0.16 D and 0.30 D for 0.04% and 0.10%, respectively). Photophobia was the most common adverse event, reported by 9.0%, 10.6% and 18.8% in 0.01%, 0.04% and 0.10% atropine respectively in 12 months and 7.8%, 8.1% and 21.1% in 24 months. These results demonstrated that in children aged 6-12 years with high myopia, nightly use of 0.10% atropine for 24 months effectively and safely attenuated myopia progression. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04699357.

Article.ArticleTitle: SARS-CoV-2-specific monoclonal antibody AER002 in Long COVID: an exploratory randomized phase 2a mechanistic trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Persistence of SARS-CoV-2 has been proposed as a biological driver of Long COVID, a disabling chronic illness with no proven treatments. We conducted an exploratory, placebo-controlled, double-blind, 2:1 randomized mechanistic trial (NCT05877508) of the SARS-CoV-2-specific monoclonal antibody AER002 in 36 participants who met the World Health Organization case definition of Long COVID. After baseline characterization, participants received a single infusion and were followed for 360 days. The primary endpoint was the PROMIS-29 Physical Health Summary Score (PHSS) at 90 days; secondary and exploratory endpoints included patient-reported and objective measures of physical and neurocognitive function as well as blood-, imaging-, and tissue-based biomarkers. While AER002 was safe and well tolerated, no significant differences in physical health, quality of life, objective measures of physical function or cognition, or blood-based biomarkers were demonstrated between the treatment and control arms. In a post-hoc analysis, participants with a lower baseline SARS-CoV-2 antibody level and higher drug exposure were more likely to perceive treatment benefit based on the Patient Global Impression of Change scale (p < 0.05 for anti-S, S1, and RBD). Although AER002 was not efficacious in this proof-of-concept study, our findings could inform future trials using monoclonal antibodies to target viral persistence in Long COVID.

Journal.Title: Digestive and liver disease : official journal of the Italian Society of Gastroenterology and the Italian Association for the Study of the Liver

Article.ArticleTitle: Comparing precutting endoscopic band ligation-assisted resection vs ESD for small gastric SMTs: a randomized controlled trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: This study evaluated the clinical feasibility of precutting endoscopic band ligation-assisted resection (precutting EBLR) for the removal of small gastric submucosal tumors originating from the muscularis propria (gSMT-MP).

This was a single-center, open-label, parallel-group randomized controlled trial (ChiCTR2200065473). All endoscopic procedures were performed by two experienced endoscopists (>300 ESD cases each). From January 2023 to December 2024, consecutive patients with gSMT-MP ≤ 16 mm were enrolled and randomly assigned to precutting EBLR or ESD. The primary outcome was operation time, additional clinical indicators were also collected and analyzed.

The median operation time was 17.5 min (range: 12-50) for the precutting EBLR group and 30 min (range: 12-80) for the ESD group. The median operation costs were $564.05 (range: $301.97-$1236.42) and $849.29 (range: $491.95-$2121.25), respectively. R0 and en-bloc resection were achieved in all patients. No delayed perforations or tumor recurrences occurred during follow-up.

Precutting EBLR demonstrated advantages in operation time compared with ESD. It represents an efficient and safe endoscopic approach for treating gSMT-MPs ≤ 16 mm, and may be potentially applicable in non-academic or lower-volume centers, pending further validation.

Journal.Title: Psychogeriatrics : the official journal of the Japanese Psychogeriatric Society

Article.ArticleTitle: The Effects of Virtual Reality Group Reminiscence Therapy on Agitation, Cognition, Depression and Social Function in Patients With Alzheimer's Disease.

Abstract.AbstractText: This study examined the impact of multisensory virtual reality (VR) group reminiscence therapy on behavioural, cognitive and psychosocial outcomes in Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, while evaluating intervention feasibility and safety.

An assessor-blinded randomised controlled trial was employed. Sixty participants with AD were randomly allocated to either the intervention group (n = 30) or the control group (n = 30). The intervention group underwent VR-based reminiscence sessions twice weekly, each lasting 40 min, for 8 weeks. The control group received routine care. Outcomes were measured before and after the intervention using the NPI-agitation subscale, Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), the 15-item Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS-15) and Short Form-36 (SF-36). Questionnaires including Presence Questionnaire (PQ), Motivation Inventory (IMI) and Virtual Reality Sickness Questionnaire (VRSQ) were used to assess intervention acceptance and side effects. The Autobiographical Memory Test (AMT) was used to evaluate memory specificity.

Post-intervention, VR participants showed markedly lower agitation scores (NPI) (4.2 ± 1.9 vs. 1.7 ± 1.2, p < 0.001), MMSE scores (23.5 ± 2.1 vs. 27.1 ± 1.4, p < 0.01), GDS-15 scores (9.8 ± 1.3 vs. 3.1 ± 1.2, p < 0.001) and SF-36 subscales of social function and mental health (both p < 0.05), compared with the control group. PQ and IMI scores indicated high acceptance of the intervention. VRSQ scores showed minor side effects (e.g., eye fatigue < 1.3). AMT results also improved significantly (event specificity: 3.2 vs. 6.2, p < 0.01).

VR group reminiscence therapy significantly improved agitation, cognition and mood in AD patients and enhanced their quality of life. The method is safe, feasible and provides a novel non-pharmacological option with an interactive and immersive experience.
